items.title: An HNN extension with its stable letter
The edge-group presentation is equivalent to the associated-subgroup presentation
items.strategy: Use injectivity to identify the edge group with its two images and transport the relators across the induced isomorphism between the associated subgroups.

items.title: HNN words, pins, and Britton-reduced words
Elementary HNN reductions preserve the represented element
items.strategy: Replace each pin by the conjugate element dictated by the defining relator and observe that this is exactly an equality in the presented group.

items.title: The transversal data used for HNN normal forms
Normal forms in an HNN extension are unique relative to chosen transversals
items.strategy: Model left multiplication followed by reduction on the set of transversal normal forms, reduce the defining relations to the published amalgam normal-form machinery, and read off uniqueness.

items.title: Britton's lemma
items.strategy: Apply the normal-form theorem to the Britton-reduced representative obtained after all elementary pin reductions and observe that a surviving stable letter forces nontriviality.

items.title: The base group embeds in its HNN extension
items.strategy: A nontrivial base-group element is already in normal form of stable-letter length zero, so Britton's lemma forbids it from collapsing to the identity.

items.title: The stable letter has infinite order
items.strategy: Every nonzero power of the stable letter is already Britton-reduced and contains a stable letter, so Britton's lemma rules out finite order.

items.title: The associated homomorphism from an HNN extension to the integers
The universal property of an HNN extension
items.strategy: Use von Dyck's theorem on the defining presentation after checking that the proposed image of the stable letter conjugates the two edge maps exactly as the relators require.

items.title: Ascending HNN extensions of injective endomorphisms
Ascending HNN extensions admit the one-sided normal form
items.strategy: Specialize the two-sided HNN normal form to the case where one associated subgroup is the whole base group and collapse the redundant transversal choice.

items.title: Higman-Neumann-Neumann: every countable group embeds in a two-generator group
items.strategy: Record the exact theorem as a source-backed waypoint only; later use would require a dedicated embedding page and is intentionally not taken here.

items.title: Cyclically Britton-reduced HNN words
Every HNN conjugacy class contains a cyclically Britton-reduced representative
items.strategy: Choose a conjugate with minimal stable-letter length and cyclically reduce one remaining pin at a time; minimality forces the process to terminate.

items.title: Cyclic permutations of a cyclically Britton-reduced HNN word stay in the same conjugacy class
items.strategy: Conjugate successively by the initial base-group and stable-letter segments and use cyclic reduction to keep the permuted word reduced.

items.title: Conjugacy between cyclically Britton-reduced HNN words reduces to base-group conjugacy after cyclic permutation
items.strategy: Compare a cyclically reduced equality after reducing the conjugator; Britton's lemma forces the minimal conjugator into the base group, and conjugating by the initial coefficient converts the result into a cyclic permutation.

items.title: Collins' conjugacy theorem for cyclically reduced HNN words
items.strategy: Pass to cyclically reduced representatives, compare stable-letter lengths by Britton's lemma, rotate one word cyclically, and finish with the base-group conjugacy reduction.

items.title: FALSE: the base group may collapse in an HNN extension
items.strategy: Refute by the embedding corollary: injective associated maps prevent any nontrivial base-group element from becoming trivial.

items.title: FALSE: every word containing a stable letter is nontrivial
items.strategy: Refute with a word containing an explicit pin whose elementary HNN reduction removes the stable letters entirely.

items.title: FALSE: HNN normal form is canonical without choosing transversals
items.strategy: Refute by comparing two different transversal choices that produce different zero-pin representatives of the same element.

items.title: FALSE: every HNN extension is an ascending HNN extension
items.strategy: Refute by choosing proper associated subgroups on both sides, so neither subgroup is the whole base group required in the ascending case.

title: Hnn Extensions and Brittons Lemma - Examples

items.title: The direct product A x Z as an HNN extension
items.strategy: Take both associated subgroups to be the whole base group with the identity isomorphism and identify the resulting presentation with A x Z.

items.title: Baumslag-Solitar groups as HNN extensions
items.strategy: Start from an infinite cyclic base group and use the associated-subgroup maps generated by multiplication by m and n.

items.title: The doubling endomorphism of Z gives an ascending HNN extension
items.strategy: Take the injective endomorphism n |-> 2n on the infinite cyclic group and compute the resulting one-sided normal forms.

items.title: Britton reduction of a word with two pins
items.strategy: Choose a word containing one positive and one negative pin and perform the elementary reductions step by step until the surviving reduced word is clear.

items.title: An HNN extension realising two conjugate subgroups
items.strategy: Adjoin a stable letter that conjugates one chosen subgroup of the base onto another and verify the resulting universal property directly from the presentation.

items.title: A word containing a stable letter need not be Britton-reduced
items.strategy: Exhibit a word with an explicit pin and show that elementary HNN reduction shortens it immediately.

items.title: An oriented graph with edge reversal
Finite simplicial paths, reduced paths, cycles, and connectedness
A simplicial tree
A simplicial graph is a tree exactly when every two vertices are joined by a unique reduced path
items.strategy: Distinct reduced paths between the same endpoints combine to a reduced cycle, and conversely any reduced cycle splits into two distinct reduced paths with common endpoints.

items.title: The simplicial path metric on the vertices of a tree
The path metric on a simplicial tree is geodesic and integer-valued
items.strategy: The unique reduced path between two vertices realises the metric, and its edge count is an integer that concatenates additively along vertices on that path.

items.title: Finite simplicial trees agree with the published finite-tree notion
items.strategy: Forget orientations to recover a finite simple graph, translate reduced simplicial paths into ordinary graph paths, and compare the two tree characterisations directly.

items.title: Graph automorphisms and group actions on a simplicial graph
Edge inversions and actions without inversions
Barycentric subdivision removes edge inversions while preserving tree actions
items.strategy: Insert a midpoint on every geometric edge, extend the action to the subdivided graph, and note that an inversion can swap the two half-edges but cannot fix either oriented half-edge.

items.title: The quotient graph of an action without inversions
Vertex and edge stabilizers fit together by incidence inclusions
items.strategy: An element stabilizing an oriented edge must stabilize both of its endpoints, so every edge stabilizer sits inside the stabilizers of the incident vertices.

items.title: Fixed subtrees and minimal invariant subtrees
The nonempty fixed-vertex set of a tree automorphism is a subtree
items.strategy: If an automorphism fixes two vertices then uniqueness of the reduced path between them forces every intermediate vertex and edge on that path to be fixed as well.

items.title: The translation length of a tree automorphism without inversions
A tree automorphism without inversions is elliptic or hyperbolic
items.strategy: Show that the integer-valued displacement function attains its infimum; zero displacement yields a fixed vertex, while positive displacement builds a unique embedded axis from successive geodesic segments.

items.title: Translation length is conjugacy-invariant and homogeneous
items.strategy: Conjugation preserves displacement values, and powers act along the same axis by repeated translations whose lengths add.

items.title: Finite groups acting on trees have a global fixed vertex after barycentric subdivision
items.strategy: Take the finite orbit hull of one vertex, reduce to a finite invariant subtree, and use its centre; barycentric subdivision turns a possible fixed edge-midpoint into a genuine fixed vertex.

items.title: Groups acting freely without inversions on trees are torsion-free
items.strategy: A torsion element generates a finite subgroup, and the fixed-point lemma then produces a fixed vertex, contradicting freeness.

items.title: Hyperbolic tree automorphisms satisfy a ping-pong criterion for freeness
items.strategy: Choose disjoint half-trees determined by the attracting directions of the hyperbolic automorphisms and apply the standard ping-pong argument on those domains.

items.title: FALSE: the published finite-tree definition already covers Bass-Serre trees
items.strategy: Refute by an infinite simplicial tree whose reduced-path behaviour is correct but whose vertex set is not finite.

items.title: FALSE: every tree action is without edge inversions
items.strategy: Refute with an action swapping the endpoints of a single edge and then contrast it with the barycentric subdivision repair.

items.title: FALSE: every tree automorphism fixes a vertex
items.strategy: Refute with a translation of the bi-infinite line, which is hyperbolic and has positive translation length.

items.title: FALSE: translation length is always the distance from an arbitrary basepoint
items.strategy: Refute by choosing a basepoint off the axis of a hyperbolic automorphism; its displacement is strictly larger than the minimum translation length.

items.title: FALSE: a quotient of a tree by a group action is always a tree
items.strategy: Refute by a free translation action on the line, whose quotient graph contains a cycle even though the original graph is a tree.

title: Simplicial Trees and Group Actions - Examples

items.title: The bi-infinite line with its translation action
items.strategy: Model the line as a simplicial tree with vertex set Z and compute the axis and translation length of the unit shift explicitly.

items.title: Regular Cayley trees of free groups
items.strategy: View the Cayley graph of a free group with respect to a free basis as a simplicial tree and read off its regular valence directly from the generators.

items.title: An edge inversion and its barycentric subdivision
items.strategy: Swap the endpoints of one edge, observe the inversion, and then subdivide once to produce an equivalent action without inversions.

items.title: A finite group fixes the centre of a finite tree
items.strategy: Take a finite symmetry group of a finite tree, compute its orbit hull, and locate the fixed centre after the possible subdivision step.

items.title: Elliptic and hyperbolic automorphisms of simplicial trees
items.strategy: Contrast a vertex-fixing symmetry with a translation along a line and compute the different translation-length behaviours side by side.

items.title: The quotient of a tree can have cycles
items.strategy: Quotient the bi-infinite line by the translation generated by one step; the quotient graph is a loop.
